Storage duration is the rule that decides how long an object's memory exists, and C++ has four of them. Automatic storage holds a local variable, destroyed at the end of its block. Static storage holds a global or a function's
local: a global is built before
the first time execution reaches it, and both last until after
object, built once per thread and destroyed when that thread ends. Dynamic storage holds an object an owner allocates, such as the elements of a

holds, and it lasts until that owner destroys it. An object's lifetime sits inside its storage duration: it starts once the constructor has returned and ends when the destructor starts, and using the object outside that span is undefined behaviour even while its memory is still there.

The problem this solves is knowing exactly when an object stops being safe to touch. A temporary, an object with no name, is destroyed at the end of the full-expression that created it, the outermost expression it belongs to, which in practice means the semicolon. Miss that boundary and you read memory that is already gone, which is what the cold check on this page tests by asking you to predict the make and drop order of a small program.

The mechanism runs in a fixed order: base classes first, then members in the order the class declares them, whatever order the constructor's initialiser list names, then the constructor body. Destruction reverses that exactly. A temporary bound directly to a reference is the one exception to its short life: the language stretches it to match the reference, a rule called lifetime extension.

What it costs is that lifetime extension is narrower than most people assume. It only fires when the temporary is bound straight to the reference variable. Pass it through a function parameter, through
, or through a range-for's hidden call, and it still dies at the semicolon while the reference or view now points at nothing.

You meet this in the robot as the gap between a lidar scan object, which is automatic, and the range readings it owns, which sit in dynamic storage until the scan itself is destroyed, and telling that gap apart for locals, statics and temporaries alike is the question this page's title is asking.

c.v: is initialised the first time execution reaches its declaration, and never again. Since C++11 that initialisation is thread-safe: if two threads reach it at the same time, one waits for the other (
). Only the initialisation is protected. Reads and writes after that need their own synchronisation.

Globals are initialised in the order they are defined within one source file. Between source files the order is unspecified, so a global whose constructor uses a global from another file can find it not yet constructed. This is the
. The standard also lets an implementation delay a global's initialisation until something in its source file is first used (
, as the cold check showed. The usual fix for the fiasco is to replace the global with a function that returns a reference to a local
, which is then built on first use. Better still, avoid the global: Core Guidelines
for no complex initialisation of the ones you keep.

You will hear "stack" and "heap" in interviews. They describe how implementations usually provide automatic and dynamic storage, and the standard uses the longer names. Either pair of words is fine in conversation, as long as you know which storage duration each one stands for.

Dynamic storage exists for two needs the others can't meet. One is a size known only at run time, as with the scan. The other is an object that must outlive the block that creates it and can't be returned by value, because its concrete type is picked at run time or because other objects hold its address.

c.v: Construction starts with the base classes, in the order they are declared. Then the members are built, in the order they are declared in the class, and the constructor body runs last. Destruction runs in exactly the reverse order: the destructor body, then the members from last to first, then the bases.
shows both halves: it is the first object built and the last one destroyed.
Locals follow the same idea at the level of a block. They are destroyed at the end of their block, in reverse order of construction. Statics are destroyed after
returns, in reverse order of when their construction finished.
